01.note: Two men made a bet: whoever could provoke Hillel into anger would win four hundred zuz. One of them chose Shabbat eve, while Hillel was washing his hair, and stood at his door calling rudely, Who here is Hillel? Each time Hillel wrapped himself, came out, called him my son, and patiently answered his insulting questions: why Babylonians have oval heads, why the people of Tadmor have bleary eyes, why Africans have wide feet. Finally the man burst out that he hoped there would not be many like Hillel in Israel, since he had lost four hundred zuz because of him. Hillel told him to watch his temper: Hillel is worth his losing four hundred zuz and four hundred more, and Hillel will not get upset.
01.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabban Gamliel calmly answered a scoffing student, and moves on to the patience of Sages. It quotes a teaching that one should always be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai; this bet is its first example.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A leading Sage, called the Nasi of Israel; a Babylonian, which the man's first question mocks.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: Named in the opening teaching as the example of an impatient man, set against Hillel.

terms.meaning: A silver coin. Four hundred zuz was a very large stake.
The title of the head of the Jewish community and its Sages in the Land of Israel.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law; the Gemara often quotes one with the words The Sages taught.

02.note: A non-Jew asked Shammai how many Torahs the Jews have. Shammai said two, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. The man said he believed in the written one but not the oral one, and asked to be converted on condition that he would be taught only the Written Torah. Shammai scolded him and threw him out. He went to Hillel, who converted him. On the first day Hillel taught him the alphabet, alef, bet, gimmel, dalet; the next day he taught it in reverse. When the convert objected that this was not what he had been told yesterday, Hillel answered: you relied on me for that, so rely on me for the Oral Torah too.
02.why: It follows the story of the man who tried to make Hillel angry, in a run of episodes setting Hillel's patience against Shammai's impatience; this is the first of three about non-Jews who came to convert.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: A Sage who scolds the would-be convert and throws him out.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A Sage who converts the man and then teaches him why he must trust oral teaching.

terms.meaning: The Written Torah is the text of the Five Books of Moses. The Oral Torah is the body of explanation and law passed down by teachers, which the Sages held was given alongside it.
The first four letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

03.note: A non-Jew came to Shammai and asked to be converted on condition that Shammai teach him the entire Torah while he stood on one foot. Shammai pushed him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand. The man then came to Hillel, who converted him and told him: what is hateful to you, do not do to another. That is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go and study.
03.why: This is the second of three stories about non-Jews who asked Shammai and then Hillel to convert them; together they illustrate the teaching that one should be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: A Sage, said here to be a builder by trade, who pushes the man away with his measuring stick.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A Sage who converts the man and sums up the Torah for him.

terms.meaning: A measuring stick a cubit long (roughly half a meter), used by builders.

04.note: A non-Jew overheard a teacher reading the list of the High Priest's garments and decided to convert so that he would be made High Priest. Shammai pushed him away; Hillel converted him and told him that only one who knows the royal protocols is made king, so go and learn them. Reading the Torah, the convert reached the verse that an outsider who comes near shall be put to death, and Hillel told him it applies even to King David. The convert reasoned that if it applies to Israel, whom God calls His firstborn, all the more to a convert who came with just his staff and bag. He blessed Hillel; later all three converts met and said Shammai's impatience sought to drive them from the world, while Hillel's patience brought them under the wings of the Divine Presence.
04.why: This third conversion story closes the run that began with the teaching to be patient like Hillel and not impatient like Shammai; the converts' own words at the end state that lesson. The Gemara then turns to other teachings about the conduct of the Sages.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: A Sage who pushes the would-be convert away.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A Sage who converts the man and guides him to see why he cannot be High Priest; the convert calls him Hillel the patient.

people.name: David
people.about: King of Israel; Hillel says even he would be put to death for this.

terms.meaning: The chief priest who served in the Temple in Jerusalem; only a descendant of Aaron could hold the role.
An argument from the lesser to the greater: if a rule applies in the milder case, it applies all the more in the stronger one.

terms.term: under the wings of the Divine Presence
terms.meaning: A phrase for becoming part of the Jewish people and coming close to God, used especially of converts.

05.note: Shmuel HaKatan fell ill with hidrokan, a swelling disease, and prayed: Master of the Universe, who can tell why this has come? He was cured. Abaye also fell ill with it, and Rava said of him: I know that Nahmani starves himself. Rava himself then fell ill with it. The Gemara asks how, since Rava was the one who said that more people are killed by the chamber pot than by starvation, and answers that the Sages forced Rava to stay in place against his will while he taught.
05.why: The Gemara has just taught that there are three kinds of hidrokan: from sin, from hunger and from witchcraft. These three cases show Sages who fell ill with it for causes other than sin.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: A Sage who fell ill with hidrokan, prayed, and was cured.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage, called Nahmani here, who fell ill with hidrokan; Rava says he starves himself.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who vouches for Abaye and later falls ill with hidrokan himself.

terms.meaning: Edema, a disease in which the body swells with fluid. The Gemara says it can be a sign of sin, or come from hunger or witchcraft.
Rava's saying means that more people die from holding in their bodily needs than from hunger.

06.note: Rabbi Yehuda praised the Romans for their markets, bridges and bathhouses; Rabbi Yosei was silent; Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai said they built them only for themselves. Yehuda, son of converts, repeated this, and the government decreed that Yehuda be elevated, Yosei exiled, and Shimon killed. Shimon and his son hid in a cave for twelve years, fed by a miraculous carob tree and spring, until Elijah announced the emperor was dead. When they came out, everything they looked at burned, and a Divine Voice sent them back for twelve months. Later Shimon cleared a doubtfully impure marketplace for priests. An old man mocked him for purifying a cemetery; Shimon looked at him and he died, then turned Yehuda, son of converts, into a pile of bones.
06.why: A teaching just quoted calls Rabbi Yehuda the head of the speakers in every place. The Gemara asks how he got that title, and this story answers: the Roman government gave it to him after he praised them.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: A Sage sentenced to death for criticizing the Romans; he hides in a cave with his son for over twelve years.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's son, who hides in the cave with him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who praised the Romans and was elevated by them as the head of the speakers in every place.

people.name: Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: He repeated the Sages' words until the government heard them.

people.name: Rabbi Pinehas ben Ya'ir
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's son-in-law, who weeps at the cracks in his skin after the cave.

terms.meaning: The biblical prophet, who in Talmudic stories appears to Sages as a messenger.
A voice from heaven that announces God's will.
A religious status, not physical dirt; contact with a dead body passes it on, and priests had to avoid it, so a place where a body might be buried was off-limits to them.
A portion of produce given to priests, which may only be grown, handled and eaten in a state of ritual purity.

07.note: The people of Tiberias ran a pipe of cold water through a channel of hot water from the town's hot springs, so the water would be warm on Shabbat. The Sages prohibited them from using it.
07.why: The Gemara is weighing two reasons why insulating food in sun-heated sand is forbidden: a decree in case people use hot ashes, or the digging involved. The Tiberias case fits the first reason but not the second, so it is raised as an objection.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which cooking and heating food are forbidden.

07.flag: The incident is only cited in passing, inside a legal objection; it has almost no events, and most of the segment is argument.

08.note: At the bathhouse of Benei Berak the openings were sealed on the eve of a Festival to keep the heat in. The next day, on the Festival, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva went in, sweated there, then came out and rinsed in the outer room. The hot water there was covered with boards. When the matter came before the Sages, they said this was allowed even where the hot water is not covered. Later, when the number of transgressors grew, they began to prohibit it. But one may walk through the large city bathhouses without concern.
08.why: A teaching has just ruled that on a Festival one may sweat in a bathhouse sealed the day before; Rabbi Yehuda brings this incident as an example, and the Gemara then explains who the transgressors were that led the Sages to forbid it.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A Sage who sweated in the Benei Berak bathhouse on a Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who sweated there with him.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which most work is forbidden, though some food preparation is allowed.
The cooler front room of a bathhouse, away from the hot water.

09.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi recalled following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi into the bathhouse on Shabbat. He wanted to set a jar of oil in the hot bath to warm it for his teacher. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him instead to take water from the bath in a secondary vessel and put the oil in that.
09.why: The Sages are debating whether heating oil on Shabbat counts as cooking. The Gemara learns three rulings from this instruction: oil can be cooked, a secondary vessel does not cook, and even warming oil counts as cooking it.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi
people.about: A student who tells the story of attending his teacher in the bathhouse.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, his teacher, who tells him how to warm the oil.

terms.meaning: A container that hot liquid has been poured into, rather than the one it was heated in. The Sages held it is not hot enough to cook.

10.note: A student of Rabbi Meir followed him into the bathhouse on Shabbat and wanted to rinse the floor. Rabbi Meir told him one may not rinse it. The student asked whether he could smear the floor with oil instead, and Rabbi Meir told him one may not smear it either.
10.why: The Gemara has asked how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could teach law inside a bathhouse, where Torah may not be discussed, and answered that stopping someone from breaking a law is different. Shmuel's report of Rabbi Meir doing the same is the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who stops his student from rinsing or oiling the bathhouse floor on Shabbat.

11.note: Rabbi Zeira wanted to move from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, so he avoided his teacher Rav Yehuda, who taught that anyone who makes that move violates a commandment. Before going he decided to hear one more teaching from him. He found Rav Yehuda in the bathhouse telling his servant: bring me natron, bring me a comb, open your mouths and let out the steam, and drink from the bathhouse water. Rabbi Zeira said that had he come only to hear this, it would have been enough. The Gemara then explains what each instruction teaches, citing a teaching on health: one who bathes in hot water and does not drink is like an oven heated outside but not inside.
11.why: The Gemara has been describing how various Sages behaved while bathing. Rav Yehuda's orders give two more lessons: everyday matters may be spoken in Hebrew in a bathhouse, and drinking and rinsing after a hot bath are good for health.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A student of Rav Yehuda who wants to move to the Land of Israel against his teacher's view.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rabbi Zeira's teacher, who held that leaving Babylonia for the Land of Israel violates a commandment.

terms.meaning: A natural mineral salt used like soap for washing.
Hebrew. Rav Yehuda gave his everyday orders in Hebrew, showing that this is allowed in a bathhouse, where holy matters are not discussed.
A command to do something, as opposed to one forbidding an act. Rav Yehuda read a verse in Jeremiah as commanding the exiles to remain in Babylonia.

12.note: Rav Avya came to Rava's house with his feet dirty with clay and put them on the bed in front of Rava. Rava was angry and wanted to torment him with hard questions. He asked why Rabba and Rav Yosef allowed moving a naphtha lamp on Shabbat. Rav Avya said it can be used to cover a vessel. Rava objected that then every pebble in the yard could be moved, since pebbles can cover a vessel too. Rav Avya answered that a lamp has the status of a vessel and pebbles do not, and he began to quote a teaching in support.
12.why: The Gemara has just reported that Rabba and Rav Yosef allowed moving a naphtha lamp on Shabbat; this story gives the reason for their ruling and tests it.

people.name: Rav Avya
people.about: A Sage who visits Rava with muddy feet and has to answer his hard questions.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage, the host, who is angered by the muddy feet on his bed.

terms.meaning: A lamp burning naphtha, a foul-smelling oil, used only for light.
Things made for use may be moved on Shabbat more freely than raw materials such as stones, which are set aside and may not be handled.

12.flag: The story stops mid-sentence (Was it not taught in a baraita that...); the quote and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak's closing remark that Rava did not embarrass Rav Avya are in the following segment.

13.note: Rabba and Rabbi Zeira visited the house of the Exilarch on Shabbat and saw a servant set a jug of cold water on the mouth of a kettle of hot water. Rabba rebuked him. Rabbi Zeira asked how this differed from setting one urn on another, which is allowed; Rabba said that urn on urn only keeps heat in, while this creates new heat. Then the servant spread a kerchief over a vat and set a cup on it, and Rabba rebuked him again. When Rabbi Zeira asked why, Rabba said: wait and see. In the end the servant wrung out the kerchief. Rabba explained that a man cares about a kerchief and will wring it, unlike an ordinary cloth.
13.why: The Gemara has just distinguished food that is only kept warm from food that is actively heated, as when placed on olive residue. Rabba's first rebuke applies the same line: keeping heat in is allowed, creating heat is not.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who twice rebukes the Exilarch's servant.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage visiting with Rabba, who asks him to explain each rebuke.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
Wringing water out of cloth is one of the kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat.

14.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting together on Shabbat when berada, a washing mixture, was brought to them. Ameimar and Rav Ashi washed with it; Mar Zutra did not. They asked him whether he did not accept Rav Sheshet's ruling that berada is permitted. Rav Mordekhai, who was there, told them not to learn from Mar Zutra, because he does not use it even on a weekday.
14.why: The Gemara has just defined berada and is discussing what may be used to wash on Shabbat. It then explains the split: Mar Zutra follows a teaching that forbids washing just to look good, while the others follow one telling a person to wash every day for the sake of his Maker.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who washes with berada on Shabbat.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who declines to wash with it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who washes with berada on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Mordekhai
people.about: Present at the scene; he explains that Mar Zutra never uses berada, even on weekdays.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage whose ruling that berada is permitted the others cite.

terms.meaning: A washing powder that the Gemara says is a mixture of aloe, myrtle and violets.

15.note: Levi sent money to Bei Hozai to buy himself a Libyan donkey. The people there tied up his money and sent it back to him along with barley, as if to say that a donkey's stride depends on the barley it eats.
15.why: The Mishna has just mentioned a Libyan donkey with an iron halter, and Rav Huna has explained the term; having mentioned the Libyan donkey, the Gemara tells this anecdote about one.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who wanted to buy a Libyan donkey.

terms.meaning: A breed of donkey prized for its quality.
A region, which the story suggests was known for its donkeys.

16.note: Levi, son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya, and Rabba bar Rav Huna were travelling together when Levi's donkey went ahead of Rabba's. Rabba bar Rav Huna was offended. To make him feel better, Levi asked him a question of law: may a badly behaved donkey like this one go out on Shabbat with a halter? Rabba answered: your father said in the name of Shmuel that the law follows Hananya.
16.why: The Gemara has just concluded, through Rav Huna bar Hiyya in Shmuel's name, that the law follows Hananya: extra restraint on an animal is not a forbidden burden on Shabbat. In this story Rabba gives that ruling to Levi, son of the man who reported it.

people.name: Levi, son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whose donkey runs ahead; he asks a question to placate his companion.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who is offended when Levi's donkey goes first, then answers his question.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage in whose name the ruling is given.

people.name: Hananya
people.about: An earlier Sage whose view, that extra restraint is not a burden, is the law.

terms.meaning: A harness of straps around an animal's head; a bit is usually enough for a donkey, so a halter is extra restraint.
On Shabbat an animal may not be made to carry a load into a public area. Gear that is not needed to control it may count as a load.

17.note: Rabbi Yehuda told of the goats of Antioch, whose udders were so large that people made pouches for them so the udders would not be scratched. A second teaching tells of a man whose wife died, leaving a nursing son. He had no money to pay a wet-nurse, so a miracle happened: he grew breasts like a woman's and nursed his son. Rav Yosef said: see how great this man was, that such a miracle was done for him. Abaye answered: on the contrary, how lowly he was, that the order of creation was changed for him. Rav Yehuda said this shows how hard it is to provide a person's food, and Rav Nahman added that miracles happen, but food has never been created by one.
17.why: The Gemara is discussing whether goats may go out on Shabbat with pouches tied to their udders, and Rabbi Yehuda's report of the Antioch goats is evidence; the story of the nursing father follows as a related teaching about breasts.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports the incident of the Antioch goats.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who praises the nursing father's greatness.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who disagrees and calls the man lowly.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who says the miracle shows how hard it is to provide food.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who adds that miracles happen but food has never been created by one.

terms.meaning: A woman paid to breastfeed another woman's baby.
The natural order of the world as God made it.

17.flag: Combines two separate passages: the Antioch goats incident and the unrelated story of the father who nursed his son.

18.note: A man married a woman who had only one arm, and he did not realize it until the day she died. Rav said: see how modest this woman was, that her husband never noticed. Rabbi Hiyya answered that this is to be expected of her, since a woman covers herself; rather, see how modest the man was, that he never noticed this about his wife.
18.why: The Gemara has just told the unusual story of a father who miraculously nursed his son, with the Sages arguing over what it says about him; it adds another unusual story over which two Sages differ in the same way.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who praises the wife's modesty.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who says the praise belongs to the husband instead.

19.note: Rav Yehuda was sitting before his teacher Shmuel when a woman came and cried out before Shmuel, and he paid no attention to her. Rav Yehuda asked him whether he did not hold by the verse that whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered. Shmuel answered: Big-toothed one, your superior will be in cold water, but the superior of your superior will be in hot water. Mar Ukva sits here as president of the court.
19.why: The Gemara has just taught that anyone able to protest wrongdoing who does not is held responsible for it, and that leaders are judged most severely. Shmuel's answer puts the duty on Mar Ukva as head of the court; the Gemara then traces that duty to the house of David.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Shmuel's student, who challenges him for ignoring the woman.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Yehuda's teacher, who ignores the woman's cry.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: The president of the court, who Shmuel says is responsible for such cases.

terms.meaning: Shmuel's image for punishment: the higher a person's authority, the harsher he is judged for failing to act.

20.note: People told Rav that a great, tall man who limped had come to Neharde'a and taught that a kelila ornament is permitted on Shabbat. Rav said: a great, tall man who limps must be Levi. From that he concluded that Rabbi Afes had died and Rabbi Hanina now sat at the head of the academy, so Levi had no one left to sit with and had come here.
20.why: The Gemara is debating whether a woman may go out on Shabbat wearing a kelila; this story reports Levi teaching that it is permitted, and the Gemara then tells how many women in Neharde'a went out wearing it after he did.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who works out from a description who the visitor is and why he came.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A great, tall Sage with a limp who taught in Neharde'a that the kelila is permitted.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: Head of the academy, who Rav concludes has died.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Who Rav concludes now heads the academy in Rabbi Afes's place.

terms.meaning: A crown-like headband worn by women, sometimes made of or set with metal; the question is whether wearing it outdoors on Shabbat counts as carrying.
